questions.q: Why does this lesson say reusing the TAD's structure for the executive presentation would lose the room within the first three slides?
options: Because an executive audience has limited time and needs business outcomes and decisions, not a walk-through of thirteen design areas in architecture-lesson order
Because the TAD contains confidential information executives aren't allowed to see
Because the TAD has no risk register section
Because executives cannot read technical documents at all
questions.explain: The executive presentation needs its own structure built around what an executive actually needs to decide, not a condensed version of the TAD's architecture-area ordering.

questions.q: How does the executive presentation state the single-org decision (Lesson 7), per this lesson's slide structure?
options: As a detailed trade-off analysis with the full reasoning from Lesson 7
It is omitted entirely from the executive presentation
As an outcome statement — 'one platform, one customer view' — rather than architecture vocabulary
As a list of governor limits affected by the decision
questions.explain: The presentation states the decision's outcome in business terms; the underlying trade-off reasoning still exists and matters, but belongs in the TAD, not the executive deck.

questions.q: How should Risk #4 (Experience Cloud scaling) be framed on the presentation's risk slide, per this lesson?
options: Using precise Salesforce licensing terminology so executives understand the technical mechanism
In business consequence terms, such as unacceptable cost or slow performance for millions of users, without technical vocabulary
It should be omitted since executives don't need to know about risks
As a direct quote from the Chapter 1 risk register table, unedited
questions.explain: The lesson's Slide 6 guidance explicitly reframes risks in business consequence terms, rather than the technical register language used internally.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say an executive audience trusts that an architecture's underlying reasoning exists without needing to personally re-derive it?
options: Because executives are not capable of understanding architecture reasoning
Because executives always personally conduct their own independent architecture review
Because the reasoning is classified and cannot be shared with executives
Because that vetting is exactly what Chapter 6's Architecture Review Board defense is for — the executive doesn't need to repeat that process
questions.explain: The lesson explains that detailed trade-off reasoning is vetted elsewhere (the ARB defense), so an executive audience can focus on consequences and trust that the underlying justification has been or will be properly examined.

questions.q: What role does this lesson say the executive presentation plays relative to Chapter 6?
options: It is the direct bridge into Chapter 6 — the artifact the CIO sponsor uses to carry the design toward the Architecture Review Board defense
It has no connection to Chapter 6 at all
It replaces the need for the Architecture Review Board defense entirely
It is only used internally by the architect and never shown to any stakeholder
questions.explain: The lesson frames this deliverable as the bridge connecting Chapter 5's completed work to Chapter 6's defense, carried forward by the executive sponsor named back in Lesson 3.
